For mobile robots to navigate unfamiliar terrain independently, they need an aerial overview of their surroundings. Current solutions primarily rely on established systems, but these fail when faced with unstructured environments due to their assumption of known world representations. Introducing HiTMap, a novel map representation, which enables robots to generate overhead views of their world by combining data from multiple layers of images. By incorporating visual and control information, HiTMap allows the robot to build maps of unfamiliar environments and deduce the location of its aerial platform. A single command can be extended to operate on multi-layered maps, making HiTMap an efficient map representation. A single overhead platform can be utilized to generate maps of unfamiliar environments, and simulations have demonstrated the effectiveness of this novel map representation in various environments.

Two-dimensional arrays of Z-complementary codes can be constructed using a combination of the Kronecker product and vectorization techniques. This construction method utilizes code sets formed by multivariable functions, specifically employing an algorithm derived from the Miller and Thomson methods. As a result, high-density inter-group complementary code sets and 2-D Z-complementary array code sets are achieved. To verify the effectiveness of the construction method, an example of an inter-group complementary code set consisting of 10 groups and 2-D Z-complementary array code set with 128 code-arrays is provided, achieving peak side lobe levels of 8 for the inter-group complementary code set and 7 for the 2-D Z-complementary array code set. Furthermore, the construction method is capable of generating array code sets with size m/2 that exhibit peak side lobe levels of log2(m/2) - 1, which represents an improvement upon previous achievements of array code sets that can be achieved with multivariable functions alone.

Computed tomography (CT) is a widely used medical imaging technique that allows doctors to visualize the interior of the body. By analyzing x-ray scans from different energy levels, CT can also identify different materials. However, traditional CT scans often produce noisy images due to limitations in the number of views. To address this issue, a new model has been developed that combines different types of total variation and curvature penalties to improve image quality. Specifically, this model uses local total variation and anisotropic total variation at different scales, as well as a higher order curvature penalty. To further enhance image quality, a separate network has been proposed to remove noise from the raw CT data. When applied to data from a multi-energy CT scanner, this model successfully produced clear images of multiple materials. To solve the complex model equations, a new algorithm has been designed based on the alternating direction method of multipliers, and demonstrates fast convergence. To demonstrate its effectiveness, researchers compared their method to a range of other techniques and found that it consistently outperforms them in terms of image quality and accuracy.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal effects impact the properties of gap plasmons in metal-nanoparticle assemblies of varying sizes, with metals made of gold and jellium. By using the random phase approximation with the model potential approach, we compare our theoretical results to an empirical boundary condition model and local density of states calculations to study the spillover and nonlocal effects in detail. Our research shows that the spillover significantly affects chemistry-dependent metals like gold, leading to shifts in resonance frequencies and broadening of linewidths when gaps are very small. Conversely, spillover has a negligible impact on physics-based metals that exhibit nonlocal effects, which exhibit a metal-like behavior in their dielectric environment.

In this research, we investigate the impact of term relevance feedback on contextual named entity retrieval. By analyzing 20 participants' term relevance feedback for 20 English news articles containing 20 entities, we identify significant patterns in term relevance feedback. These include a preference for content words, function words, and exploring new content words. Notably, we found that n-grams of length 1 to 3 are the most frequently selected by participants. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating these feedback patterns into content-based text ranking improves contextual n-gram retrieval for English news articles, achieving significant improvements with 3 rounds of iterative feedback.

The analysis of multivariate time series and longitudinal data is often
complicated by the need to convey a large amount of information in detail,
driving the development of interactive visualization techniques. However,
existing visualization methods struggle to support the complex mental processes
required when the data has changing values. Through a combination of literature
review and observational analysis, we discovered that when exploring such data,
users switch between examining various aspects, such as how values change over
time and how individual data points relate to each other. Based on this
understanding, we developed the Enabling Interactivity on Multivariate Time
Series (EITs) system, an interactive visualization system designed to meet the
needs of EITs users, and we demonstrated its effectiveness in a case study using
an actual dataset.

The electronic health record (EHR) is a widely used information system in healthcare, which contains a treasure trove of information. However, the unstructured nature of these records poses a significant challenge to data analysis. A novel approach, the Heterogeneous Similarity Graph Neural Network (HSGNN), is introduced to address this issue. The HSGNN framework converts the clinical data into a complex graph structure, enabling the use of a new method for data extraction and drug recommendation. A key component of the HSGNN is a new architecture that combines multiple graph processing techniques and node feature functions. Extensive experimentation on EHR datasets reveals that the HSGNN is highly effective at making accurate drug recommendations even for rare diseases.

This study explores the impact of solvent effects on the behavior of an electric double layer surrounding a charged soft surface immersed in an electrolyte solution. Using a mean-field approach, we develop a comprehensive framework that integrates the influence of solvent influence on polymer chain behavior using the Flory-Huggins parameter, χ. By applying the Boltzmann energy distribution and a suitable boundary value problem, we obtain an analytical solution that reveals the influence of solvent on charge distribution within the electric double layer. Notably, considering only solvent influence on ions is insufficient; solvent influence on polymer chains must be taken into account as well.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of software engineering is a long-standing goal, with few areas more exemplifying this than software engineering requirements (SRs) which are often documented in unstructured formats by developers. To address this challenge, we investigated whether machine learning techniques could be applied to automatically generate SRs from textual documents. Our study involved creating a structured dataset of SRs annotated with text passages, which was then used to evaluate three distinct approaches: fine-tuning a pre-trained transformer model on the full SR text, incorporating attention mechanisms to link SRs with text snippets in a knowledge graph model, and leveraging meta-learning for few-shot SR generation. Our experiments revealed that the pre-trained transformer model achieved the best results, with a high ROUGE score of 0.46, closely matching the performance of human annotators. Additionally, we conducted a user study demonstrating that the majority of users preferred the generated SRs over those annotated by humans in terms of quality and coherence.

This research focuses on developing an energy-efficient technique within a network coding system, using a multi-user relay network, to support high data rates with minimal power consumption. The study involves a global objective function, balancing rate and consumption at each user. A scheduling method is used, with a power distribution algorithm optimizing energy usage for each user. The proposed algorithm converges to a local optimum under specific conditions, and its performance is compared to other methods. The results show its effectiveness in improving energy efficiency within network coding systems.

A theoretical framework combining the Dirac equation with the use of relativistic pseudopotentials and plane waves has been employed to study the structure and properties of antisymmetric and symmetric Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states formed by a localized magnetic moment on a superconductor surface. This study specifically examines the interaction of an Mn adatom and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface, with results showing that the desired in-gap states are strongly influenced by the spin configuration and position of the adsorbate atoms. For certain configurations, such as an Mn atom at the bridge site, significant charge accumulation is found in the region between the adsorbate atom and the substrate, and a strong coupling with the substrate leads to a broadening of the in-gap states. Additionally, a dimerized Mn adsorbate system is found to exhibit a significant increase in these in-gap states, with a characteristic "breathing" spin configuration observed at a specific adsorption site. Furthermore, a significant correlation is found between the observed magnetic moments of the adsorbate atoms and their position on the substrate, with a significant reduction in moment observed at a specific adsorption site.

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) are commonly used
for robot localization, offering a balance between speed and accuracy. However,
the position of the robot is often influenced by the reference pose of the scan
used to model the environment, leading to localization inaccuracies. In this
paper, a novel method is presented that utilizes a deep neural network (DNN) to
create a mapping between NDT models and their corresponding correct pose
positions, effectively reducing reference-related reference biases. The proposed
method is based on a simplified position-to-position NDT approach, still retaining
the efficiency of traditional techniques. Through an extensive evaluation on
a large dataset of outdoor urban scans, it has been demonstrated
that the method significantly enhances localization accuracy, with a mean
localization error reduction of 10%.

Satellite images are widely used in various fields, particularly for monitoring the Earth's surface. Deep networks have been successfully applied to satellite image analysis, but they require substantial computational resources and expertise to implement. This paper presents a novel algorithm for identifying object edges in satellite images, demonstrating the algorithm's effectiveness through a rigorous mathematical proof. The proposed solution is not only comparable to state-of-the-art deep network approaches but also can be applied to a broader range of images, including those with a more limited resolution. Additionally, the paper showcases the versatility of this method by applying it to multiple satellite image datasets, while highlighting its potential benefits over deep network architectures.

Researchers have recently used X-ray Absorption Near Edge Spectroscopy (XANES) at an advanced synchrotron source to study the fine structures of absorption spectra of materials near their edges. High-fluence X-ray pulses enable the observation of dynamic changes in the angular distribution of photoabsorption, which are influenced by the population of excited electrons. This study proposes a model that can accurately reproduce these complex spectral features by considering a group of excited electrons and their interactions with core holes, core excitons, and the radiative and non-radiative decay rates. This versatile model can be applied to reproduce a variety of experimental data from different elements and the periodic table.

The application of a Deep Neural Network (DNN) in modulating a signal and employing a fixed classification scheme offers robustness against interference and noise. However, its susceptibility to a type of attack known as an adversarial attack is a significant concern. In a type of additive adversarial attack, the adversary modifies the transmitted signal to mislead the DNN into incorrect classification. To counter this, a mixture of two generative adversarial networks (MGAN) is developed. The MGAN consists of a Signal Generator Network (SGN) that creates a signal in the presence of interference and noise to maximize the probability of correct classification by the Discriminator Network (D). The SGN then trains another network to replicate its generated signal based on the learned probability distribution. The proposed MGAN outperforms GAN in countering a form of blind adversarial attack in numerical simulations.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is a complex task due to the
irregular shapes, colors, and sizes of the lesions, as well as the challenges
arising from inter-institutional data. A recent approach, ComselNet, has been
developed to tackle this issue, but it relies on specific training datasets.
To overcome this limitation, we introduce the use of Experience Replay within
Experience Free Continual Learning to adapt ComselNet when encountering new
datasets. Additionally, we also investigate the performance of Experience
Free Contincon, ComselNet without Experience Replay, and the effect of
continual learning on model performance.

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to the Cheeger-Bishop-Arithmetic gap is introduced, drawing from bipolar geometry. In the Bipolar Theorem, certain conditions under which the upper and lower metrics coincide is determined, similar to the original theorem. Additionally, a connection is established between cohomology and the alignment of a manifold's mean curvature.

Modeling complex phenomena often involves creating mathematical models, but traditional approaches can't always achieve high accuracy due to limitations in computational resources and model simplifications. To improve accuracy, we can use data-driven techniques like machine learning to refine models and increase their predictive power. However, there's a challenge in selecting the most effective mathematical model to update since traditional model types can't easily distinguish which parts of the model are most important for predictive purposes. To address this issue, we've developed a new framework called ML-MME that utilizes machine learning to update the error of dynamical models. By leveraging this method, we've found that it's crucial to consider the underlying model structure and use it to guide model refinement for better predictive performance. To test our method's capabilities, we've applied it to two real-world mathematical models, including a semiconductor device model and a gas-phase reaction model. Our results show that while using the same neural network to approximate both model functions yields similar results, applying the method consistently within a specific mathematical model leads to more accurate predictions. Moreover, we've observed that incorporating existing model knowledge can help differentiate between functions and lead to more effective predictive outcomes.

A key question in the formation of massive stars remains unanswered. 
The central parts of young, massive star-creating cores, called hot cores, are
characterized by high temperatures and specific molecular emission. 
The temperature and molecular emission in hot cores are thought to result from
massive star formation. 
This study uses ALMA data to examine how the core of Dragon-106 changes over
time. 
Data from ALMA reveals that Dragon-106 consists of a central core surrounded by
a large envelope. 
A new, hot core-like source, DR106C2, has been found in the core of Dragon-106. 
This new source has the same size as the existing hot core, DR106C1, but is
spatially separate. 
The two sources, DR106C1 and DR106C2, share similar emission from CO+, 
indicating that they share similar physical conditions. 
This suggests that the new source, DR106C2, is forming a second, massive star. 
Future research will be needed to determine if the two sources, DR106C1 and DR106C2, 
are part of a binary system.

A theoretical primordial black hole dark matter model is proposed, which forms from primordial black holes that collide with stars, extracting material and eventually triggering supernovae. These supernovae produce heavy elements necessary for the development of life. To study this theory, simulations are conducted using the PopSyCLE code, which models the life cycles of binary star systems, if they explode as supernovae, and if they merge to form black holes. To obtain primordial black holes of various sizes, we simulate over 1000 systems, each consisting of 15 stars. We also assess the plausibility of such a dark matter theory by analyzing its implications for early galaxy formation, which are compared with existing observations.

This study examines equilibrium states of a system of uniform wedge-shaped molecules, consisting of three spherical components, where the splay angle is denoted by $2\alpha$. Through Monte Carlo simulations, we observed that splay-modulated phases emerge in two distinct forms: one featuring a planar modulation and the other a screw-like structure. Our simulation results indicate that the splay angles of these nonliquid states are solely determined by the splay angles of the wedge-shaped molecules. Additionally, we found that the splay structure transitions to the liquid state as the density of the system increases.

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize adjustments to a pre-trained model for a specific task, adapting only a minimal set of parameters, in contrast to adjusting the entire model. We propose introducing a single special token and fine-tuning just this token and the final layer of the model for classification tasks, resulting in a more compact and performant model with respect to fine-tuning scenarios and adaptation with respect to in-context learning. We tested this approach on various benchmarks including sentence classification and in-context learning with state-of-the-art language models, including those with 175 billion parameters. We found that our method, using a single special token and fine-tuning the final layer, is on par with state-of-the-art methods like LoRA and adapter fusion for sentence classification tasks, achieving near 100% performance. Additionally, our method outperformed other special token-based approaches in fine-tuning and adaptation with respect to in-context learning, including those with 175 billion parameters.

This paper explores a complex problem, rooted in everyday experiences and business processes, of evaluating items based on their added value when combined with other elements. To address this challenge, we introduce a Markov chain framework that considers the inherent connections between preferences and proposes an approach that enhances its performance by comparing it to a baseline method. The proposed method demonstrates superior results on both artificially created and real-world datasets.

Our approach to analyzing polymer liquid behavior relies on the concept of configurational entropy, which we use to predict transitions between different states of matter. An ordinary glass transition can be analogized to a localized transition, whereas a polymerization process significantly alters the thermodynamic characteristics and results in a more pronounced transition. However, this analogy has its limitations, primarily due to the different nature of the transitions involved. Normal glass transitions affect motion without altering structure, whereas polymerization also significantly impacts structure. An initial stage of transition is driven by the reduction of configurational entropy, which is distinct from the subsequent stage where a more pronounced change in structure occurs. By focusing on the configurational entropy change, we can identify a new indicator known as the 'local entropy temperature,' which is unique to the first stage of the process. This concept provides a different perspective on the transition, differentiating it from the conventional view of the second stage, which is associated with the spinodal line.

Transformer-based language models have achieved significant success in negation negation tasks, leading to the question of whether these models truly comprehend the concept of negation. This study investigates negation and negation negation processing in Transformer models using a range of examples, including those with familiar and novel words. Notably, our results show that while these models grasp negation with known words, they struggle to extend their understanding to new lexical items, indicating limited theoretical understanding of negation. Furthermore, to explore whether these models account for content within a negated clause, we developed developmentally-appropriate games and incorporated them into evaluation datasets. This comparative analysis between our models and human children reveals that top-performing models struggle with the complexities of negation, as human performance significantly surpasses machine results, even at advanced ages. Ultimately, this research contributes a comprehensive developmental dataset for negation negation, facilitating the evaluation of natural language understanding across both human and artificial agents.

A significant limitation of attention in neural machine translation is its reliance on source context, hindering the generation process to some extent. To address this issue, this paper introduces novel attention mechanisms that consider source context as well as future target context. The proposed mechanisms, referred to as "look-ahead attention," are designed to improve generation by predicting future targets using current context, with potential benefits including reduced computation and streamlined modeling. Experimental results, however, show that look-ahead attention yields better generation without computation overhead. Specifically, a simple prediction model, looking ahead by one target word, achieves significant gains, offering a promising direction for increased model efficiency.

This passage specifically examines the Kontsevich weights of diagrams representing a connection and curvature formula for symplectic $\mathfrak{sl}(n)$-Poisson structures, with an effective, though not highly optimized, method for computing these weights provided, allowing for a curvature graph diagram to determine the potential of an $n$-ple potential.

This research explores large N, λ deformations of a complex CFT, specifically O(N) spin models, through their thermodynamic properties. It examines how specific changes affect thermal and entangment entropy in specific dimensions, specifically 1+1 or 2+2. It demonstrates that, specifically in 1+1, a certain behavior, a large drift in an entropy measure, persists, linking it to a change in a critical index, γ. Conversely, this measure does not appear when examining how entanglement behaves in specific dimensions, specifically 2+2. It also shows that, this measure does not appear when examining how entanglement behaves in specific dimensions, specifically 2+2. It discusses possible explanations for this phenomenon and how it might be explained through an action method.

Our research examines the technical requirements of the paper "A General Framework for Pricing Asian Options Under Markov Processes" by Hu, Li, and Yu, published in the International Journal of Theoretical Finance in 2019. Unfortunately, the source code and key equations for the full payoff options presented in that study were neither provided nor published, and our analysis reveals errors in the closed-form equations for knock-in and knock-out Asian options. Moreover, the call/put options equations contain erroneous placeholder values for variance $\sigma^2$ and strike price $K$. Consequently, our work rectifies the incorrect equations and provides alternative approaches for pricing knock-in/knock-out Asian options, ultimately offering fast and accurate pricing solutions.

The discovery of diffuse gamma-ray emission from clusters of galaxies by Fermi-LAT in 2015 sparked significant interest. Our simulations of this type of emission reveal that it primarily originates from high-energy electrons produced by proton-proton collisions between the intracluster medium and cosmic rays. This process, which occurs within the cluster's dense environment and its halos, generates a gamma-ray flux that aligns with Fermi-LAT's observations. The associated emission from inverse Compton and hadronic processes can be distinguished through their unique energy spectra and morphological characteristics, such as the lack of pi^0 decay signal in certain observation sites. The morphological pattern of this emission is influenced by both the cluster mass distribution and the distribution of cosmic rays.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can create distinct patterns in the correlation functions of these models, specifically in their oscillating signatures. Research into the collider physics of these models, specifically second-order perturbations, has provided valuable insights that can be probed with current data from the Cosmic Microwave Background. Our analysis builds upon this research, focusing on two previously unexplored aspects: classical dynamics beyond the linear approximation and higher-order correlation functions, specifically the fourth order. We find that these aspects are consistent with their quantum counterparts, providing a framework for understanding the primordial features' physics. We propose that cross-checking quantum and classical correlation functions can provide strong evidence for a specific primordial feature model. Our analysis includes detailed studies of primordial features' physics, specifically how their power spectra and correlation functions evolve and what implications this has for inflationary models. Our findings suggest that classical correlation functions can provide a powerful tool for understanding the primordial features' physics, specifically for modes that have not been previously explored.

Despite their impressive performance, deep convolutional neural networks remain difficult to interpret, particularly their convolutional layers, which are a primary source of ambiguity. This paper introduces a new technique for visualizing and understanding these networks by displaying how features in these layers correlate with activation patterns, focusing on linking filters to specific images and words from a dictionary derived from the network's input images and corresponding labels. This approach generates a three-dimensional model that maps filters to spatial regions in images and associated words, which can be interactively explored in 3D. By using this model, users can identify activated filters in a given image, examine their spatial activation patterns, and explore associated words, while also analyzing the network's behavior on random inputs to discover salient concepts.

Developing a comprehensive understanding of cuprate superconductivity is of great importance. A recent study has revealed a previously unexplored phenomenon, long-range attraction between electrons in one-dimensional (1D) systems that occurs due to interactions with phonons. Specifically, the interaction has been observed via both the $B_{1g}$ and $B_{2g}$ apical oxygen channels. By applying this interaction to non-doped cuprates, researchers found an approximate critical temperature for the transition to a different phase, and discovered that a different mechanism is at play compared to other materials.

The adoption of graphical models in causal learning has grown due to their ability to represent uncertain knowledge and handle network model ambiguities. Research on learning causal structures from datasets has been explored extensively, but this study focuses on developing a new method that incorporates clinical knowledge and reduces reliance on statistical models. The proposed approach uses the dataset's high conditionality and clinical expertise to infer causal structures, resulting in a graphical model that accurately reflects the causal structure of a study on myocardial infarction and related factors.

Magnetic fields of up to 100 Tesla in three dimensions were used to explore the phase diagram of the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ at temperatures ranging from 4 to 300 K. Our in-situ neutron diffraction analysis revealed that an applied magnetic field causes a significant change in the periodic lattice of magnetic skyrmions at $B_{t0\perp} \approx 35$ Tesla, as opposed to the Co$_9$Mn$_2$Pd$_2$ skyrmion lattice's shift at $B_{t0\perp} \approx 45$ Tesla. This distinct behavior highlights the critical influence of chemical composition on the topological properties of these materials.

This article provides an overview of sophisticated dynamic factor models, specifically in high-dimensional settings. These models are capable of capturing intricate relationships between a multitude of interconnected variables, such as economic data, with applications spanning across the social and natural sciences. We begin by introducing the fundamentals of dynamic factor models, followed by an examination of recent advancements, specifically innovative modeling techniques and forecasting strategies, to high-dimensional systems. Finally, we identify the most pressing lines of future research within this field.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints.

Recent advancements in deep learning have made neural networks a preferred choice in the realm of reversible steganography. Specifically, Bayesian neural networks have been found to be particularly effective due to their ability to model uncertainty and provide more accurate network outputs. This has enabled the classification of host images into relevant and overfilled categories with greater precision. Our research focuses on developing a Bayesian neural network-based framework for reversible steganography and demonstrates that this setup can classify host images into the correct category with 100% accuracy and also allows for accurate image reconstruction from overfilled images with a high reconstruction rate of 99.13%.

The primary goal of mean-field theory in dynamo models is to create simplified, two-dimensional representations of three-dimensional processes. In particular, this simplified approach allows for an increased understanding of turbulent effects, which are crucial in explaining observed astrophysical phenomena. In this research, we explore the effects of turbulent influence on global convective dynamos, specifically focusing on rotation and tidal forces. By conducting numerical simulations and comparing them to mean-field models, we aim to identify the necessary components to achieve agreement. To our knowledge, this study is the first to utilize direct calibrations of turbulent effects, rather than phenomenological parameters. We find that to accurately account for the effects of global rotation and tidal forces on mean-field models, it is necessary to consider the entire turbulent influence spectrum, not just the traditional alpha and beta effects. Moreover, our study reveals that global convective dynamos are more complex and require a deeper investigation to accurately capture their behavior.

A study has been conducted on the molecular line spectrum of the starburst galaxy NGC4945 using the ALMA telescope, focusing on both the 2.6 and 3.3 millimeter wavelengths. The observations revealed the presence of molecular hydrogen cyanide, as well as carbon monoxide emission, which indicates a powerful outflow of gas from the galaxy. The data showed multiple layers of this outflow, with velocities exceeding the galaxy's systemic velocity by a significant margin. The energy required to drive this outflow was calculated to be approximately 10 to the power of 40 ergs per year, which is consistent with the output of massive stars. The ALMA imaging also revealed that a significant portion of the outflow was concentrated at the galaxy's center, with gas velocities that varied depending on distance from the galaxy. The data was analyzed to determine the density and temperature of the gas, as well as the geometry of the outflow. The results suggest that the outflow is primarily driven by the supernovae of massive stars, with a significant role played by the star formation process.

A simplified version of the original quasilinear formalism is often used for its computational efficiency in analyzing magnetized plasmas, particularly in magnetized turbulence and plasma turbulence studies. However, this approach can violate basic physical principles like energy conservation and current conservation. A new conservative formulation is proposed, incorporating a conservative finite element method based on the Galerkin approach. Analytical expressions for necessary coefficients are derived to facilitate the approach. These developments are first verified through analytical and numerical comparisons with the traditional quasilinear model for a basic test case involving a shear Alfvén wave and a white-in-velocity kinetic model. Moreover, this conservative formulation is applied to study the nonlinear evolution of Alfvénic turbulence using the 2D slab geometry.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SDIMSIMs. We derive and analyze these methods, and then use Newton-Kottler iteration to create strategies for controlling error and adjusting step sizes in these methods. We demonstrate and evaluate the performance of a specific variable stepsize SDIMSIM with order of accuracy four, and compare it to a traditional approach, where traditional second derivative general linear methods are used in conjunction with Newton-Kottler integration and adaptive step size controls.

We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific binary quadratic inequality involving C1 and R C1 semigroup generators. The relationship shows that T being exponentially stable is equivalent to the existence of a strictly positive C1 x* or RC1 x* solution of this inequality. Furthermore, we present a method for constructing C1 x* or RC1 x* solutions of a specific binary quadratic inequality, involving the use of R-C1 x* or C1 semigroup R and C1 semigroup S, both being exponentially stable.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a software application designed to compute the interaction between dimuonium particles and matter environments. The interaction between dimuonium and matter is characterized by two primary parameters: the cross section and energy transfer rates, which MuMuPy is designed to quantify. In a dimuonium-Matter interaction, dimuonium either scatters off its environment with a cross section proportional to $1/\beta^2$, or it becomes trapped within atomic structures, where the transferred energy is utilized to ionize surrounding atoms. Notably, dimuonium-Matter interactions are distinct in that they generate ionized atoms, which can be detected, and thus provide a means to determine the properties of dimuonium.

Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to a benchmark, a process known as relative portfolio performance, in contrast to tracking how individual stocks perform. The goal of achieving outperformance is driven by the need for higher returns and can be more challenging than simply tracking the market. In this context, we propose a portfolio optimization framework based on performance metrics that compare a portfolio's total wealth to its reference wealth, while also considering the spread between the two. By employing a power utility function, we derive optimal portfolios for simple and complex financial models, including scenarios with many stocks. Notably, we find that return maximization strategies in these financial models are consistent with our proposed approach, although we highlight the limitations of focusing solely on return, especially in terms of risk considerations.

The most abundant galaxy type in the universe is dwarf galaxies, which are characterized by extremely low metal concentrations. These abundant yet poorly understood objects hold significant implications for the development of the universe's structure. I'll examine the characteristics of the gas within dwarf galaxies and how they influence the evolution of star formation in these objects. I'll also explore potential solutions to existing issues within these galaxy models, addressing existing discrepancies in observational data. The examination will encompass multiple areas, including local group studies, observations of star activity, chemical composition, the impact of supernovae explosions, and gas outflows. These dwarf galaxies serve as natural laboratories for studying the evolution of the universe, and I'll investigate existing problems and offer possible solutions.

We investigate the quasiparticle collapse phenomenon, which occurs when quasiparticles lose their distinct characteristics due to interactions with local bosons in a specific model. Focusing on fermionic quasiparticles, we demonstrate through the self-consistent bosonization approach and a non-local self-energy framework that their collapse is typically rare. Furthermore, we examine the quasiparticle collapse within the context of an electron collapse model at the Kondo breakdown point.

Golan and Sapir \cite{MR3335383} initially established that the divergence in Thompson's group $F$ grows at least as fast as $n^{(\frac{1}{2}+ \varepsilon)}$. Building on this, our research demonstrates that the same lower bound applies to the divergence in the braided Thompson groups with indices greater than or equal to 3, as well as in the generalized Thompson groups with index greater than or equal to 2, confirming the same for the braided Thompson group with index 1.

This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture, including the DPR retriever, for a question-answering task, with the goal of outperforming the full Transformer approach. We provide a comprehensive comparison between RAG and the full Transformer approach, and present our implementation built on the HuggingFace/transformers library, making the code accessible for future research. Notably, our implementation fine-tunes the DPR retriever and BERT QAS models jointly, requiring the entire architecture to be present in the training process. We also show the effectiveness of a batch retrieval method in our implementation. Experimental results reveal that jointly fine-tuning the DPR retriever and BERT QAS model yields better performance than pre-trained retrievers, and are supported by the accompanying code and model available at https://github.com/m-ritter/rag-end-to-end-finetune.

This study derives a new set of recurrence coefficients for the asymptotic behavior of polynomials that are orthogonal with respect to a logarithmic weight given by $q(x) = |x|^{\alpha} e^{-\lambda |x|}$. The investigation focuses on the properties of the coefficients, particularly those that are independent of the parameter $\lambda$. By deriving the precise recurrence coefficients, we establish a product formula for the polynomials and derive asymptotic expressions for both the polynomials and their Christoffel-Birkhoff expansions in two distinct regimes: inside the support interval and outside of it. The results are shown to confirm the presence of a limiting equilibrium measure predicted by R.R. Hall's research.

Summation of text is a fundamental and crucial skill, extensively researched in the
field of Natural Language Processing. The evaluation of this skill by humans is
a complicated task, especially when assessing various levels of summary quality.
To address this challenge, a group of 500 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers were
recruited and trained on annotation guidelines, with the goal of identifying
additional, qualified workers who can provide reliable quality assessments.
The research presented here shares the outcomes of the recruitment process and
the methods employed to identify qualified workers for human assessment of
summaries, including the creation of a new, simplified annotation guideline and
a filtering method based on English proficiency and age.

Text-video retrieval, an essential task in artificial intelligence research and practical applications, has been a significant focus for researchers and industry professionals. The increasing complexity of video content, however, poses a significant challenge to its effective processing. In response to this challenge, we developed TS²-Net, a transformer-based approach designed to improve text-video retrieval. The TS²-Net model employs two key innovations to enhance performance: 1) a token shift mechanism inspired by transformers, which dynamically reorders and combines video tokens to capture more meaningful relationships between text and video tokens, and 2) a token selection mechanism that selectively extracts critical visual tokens based on their similarity to text embeddings, thereby reducing the impact of irrelevant content. The results of our experiments demonstrate that TS²-Net significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with practical implications in terms of improved computational efficiency.

We've examined neutral flavor-changing currents within the Standard Model and discovered that they produce negligible effects, yet in the Standard Model's extended versions, they can be more pronounced, prompting the need for theoretical predictions and experimental verifications. Our research focused on two specific extensions: a lepton-number changing Higgs singlet and a lepton-Higgs doublet doublet scenario, where the latter allows for neutral flavor-changing currents involving the top quark. In the lepton-Higgs doublet scenario, several key observables, such as the CP-violating electron dipole moment of the top quark, Higgs production and decay rates, and top quark electric dipole moment, were investigated through one-loop calculations. To address the complexity of our models, we developed a simplified, effective field theory that encompasses all possible dimension-5 and dimension-6 operators, matching the parameters of the full models to the effective theory's parameters. Our research revealed that a lepton-Higgs doublet scenario with viable parameters can result in significant effects on the electric dipole moment, CP-violating electron dipole moment, and Higgs production and decay rates, even though the lepton-Higgs doublet scenario violates certain constraints on lepton flavor universality in beta decays.

In this paper, we investigate a hybrid model of network formation, combining the preferential attachment and uniform attachment models. This orientation of the network is directed, and its size is infinite. We find conditions that guarantee the existence of a network process satisfying the given orientation and degree distributions, and we demonstrate a method for generating a network process with a specific degree distribution. This method is based on a delayed approach to network formation. Additionally, we show the probability of generating a network process with a particular out-degree distribution, and we prove the probability is non-zero if and only if the variance of the moment generating function of the degree is finite.

The expanding utilization of unlicensed frequency bands necessitates innovative wireless communication technologies to boost available bandwidth. However, the proliferation of devices in these areas may result in interference between multiple transmit and receive pairs. Consequently, identifying multiple links and estimating their quality parameters is essential. In our proposed solution, a multi-task learning framework is designed, combining joint link identification and characterization with direction of arrival estimation. To facilitate this approach, a comprehensive dataset comprising interferences and noise signals across multiple frequency bands and spatial configurations was created. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution, a Convolutional Neural Network model was implemented, yielding accurate results in identifying multiple links and estimating their quality parameters.

To grasp the impact of gravitational force on both quantum systems moving at varying speeds and their associated probabilities, researchers have made efforts to understand how gravity affects quantum behavior. This knowledge contributes to a broader understanding of how gravity influences quantum mechanics. This study examines how a specific property called "electric charge" is affected by a particular aspect of space-time known as "dislocation." The study considers a scenario where space-time dislocation is not just timelike but also spatial, making it non-trivial. To explore this, the study looks at how a particular property known as "non-geometric phase" affects both the movement speed and energy of a quantum particle with mass and shows a correlation between these two properties. This study's approach can be applied to other quantum properties and helps shed light on the relationship between a quantum system's movement and its energy levels.

Countable, locally standard measure algebras and their isomorphism problems are examined. Research on this topic continues the investigation into when the isomorphism of measure algebras holds, specifically focusing on the case where a subalgebra is involved. Building on previous work, it has been established that for any infinite cardinal $\kappa$, the collection of all measure-algebras with Lebesgue measure less than $\kappa$ derived from $\kappa$ many real-valued functions is $\Sigma^1_1$ in the space of such algebras. Moreover, we investigate the conditions under which these algebras, specifically those consisting of functions whose supports have measure less than $\kappa$, are not monadic Borel in terms of the operations of such algebras.

This study aims to assess the feasibility of measuring the polarization state of the proton. By analyzing the electron-photon correlation following a Compton scattering event, the proton's polarization can be identified, which plays a significant role in the electron's spin-dependent cross-sections in Deeply Virtual Compton Scattering. Furthermore, the paper presents an estimated difference in this polarization observable between nucleon and nuclear targets, which could help resolve the long-standing "missing contribution" conundrum in the light nuclei nuclear transverse momentum distribution analysis.

All AI systems have a fundamental problem in that their predictions can't be
evaluated or corrected by people. 40 years ago, researchers addressed this
issue by designing AI systems that provided multiple possibilities along with
their respective probabilities. This enabled humans to assess and modify the
systems accordingly. Following the success of machine learning, researchers
re-evaluated this problem and developed novel methods to boost performance and
verify the reliability of AI systems, particularly in high-stakes situations.
However, the current approaches are limited to the field of probabilistic
machine learning and lack unified frameworks to improve AI systems through
human input. This paper presents an integrated framework to enhance AI
systems by combining multiple forms of human feedback, drawing inspiration from
the field of human-AI collaboration research. This new framework can utilize
various human interactions, such as selecting preferred options, correcting
errors, and providing additional information, to improve the performance of AI
systems based on reinforcement, probabilistic, and learning-from-critique AI
models. This comprehensive model is then demonstrated through a series of
practical examples to illustrate its effectiveness and versatility.

Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of the superfluid state in a one-dimensional spin-orbit coupled bosonic system through numerical analysis. We utilize the Time-Evolving Block Decimation algorithm to analyze the quantum many-body trimers. As the temperature increases, the superfluid transitions into a normal thermal state, and our analysis shows that it passes through an intermediate metastable regime. This metastable regime is initially characterized by a first-order thermal transition where the superfluid directly transitions to a normal phase. With further temperature increase, the metastable regime becomes longer, and secondary phase transitions occur, initially giving way to a modulated superfluid with antiferromagnetic properties in the long-wavelength limit. As the temperature continues to rise, the modulated superfluid transitions into a normal phase, marking a second-order thermal transition.

Consider two groups, G and H. A degeneration from G to H occurs when a sequence of groups, G_n, is defined such that both G_n to H_n and G_n to H_n converge as n becomes very large. This paper proves two main points: Firstly, the possible outcomes of such a degeneration sequence are limited to a small number of groups in comparison to the total number of possible groups, a finding that holds particular relevance for the case where the group order is e^(5k). Secondly, a group of realizable graphs can only be formed by the automorphism group of a finite abelian group of order at most e^(k^2+o(k^2)). To achieve these results, we employed tools from representation theory, particularly the Peter-Weyl theorem.

Recently, two cases involving non-supersymmetric pairs of theories in two dimensions were identified. These pairs consist of chiral theories paired with unitary theories, whereas another type of pair features two unitary theories, which can be constructed from boundary flows in AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ when the AdS$_2$ region is truncated. Researchers have previously explored such scenarios in cases with supersymmetry, resulting in pairs where both theories are unitary. We present three new scenarios involving AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ duality. These involve pairs of theories that are non-supersymmetric and possess either a chiral and a unitary theory, or two unitary theories. These three cases specifically utilize Type IIA supergravity solutions with massive gravity.

In numerous machine learning tasks, particularly those involving Gaussian Process regression, the choice of kernel functions is crucial. This study aims to automatically discover kernel functions that can be applied broadly, by utilizing genetic programming on a vast dataset of randomly generated functions. Our results indicate that certain basic mathematical functions consistently produce the best outcomes. Furthermore, the proposed approach is able to adapt well to different problems, and the selected kernel functions show substantial performance gains compared to previously developed Gaussian Process kernels.

Future high-energy muon colliders face a challenge in mitigating background events caused by collimator and beam pipe debris generated by muon-matter interactions. These background events hinder the detection of rare physics processes, making background reduction a crucial step in the design process. This tutorial, based on an open-source Python code called BEAMIND, provides a comprehensive introduction to the development of strategies for background mitigation at muon colliders using Monte Carlo simulations of secondary particle interactions.

Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with reduced computational requirements and enhanced data privacy through blocked weight pruning. This method leverages a differentiable pruning technique based on optimal transportation theory, thus enabling gradient descent. By utilizing a discrete entropy regularization, we achieve efficient implementation. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach offers superior performance in comparison to state-of-the-art blocked pruning methods across various architectures, especially when the pruning ratio is 80%. Furthermore, we find that the choice of entropy regularization is a crucial factor in the success of our approach.

The presence of a disorder potential within a Bose-Einstein condensate leads to the formation of localized modes and the emergence of single-particle exclusion, or Pauli blocking. When a Bose gas exhibits phase-stiffness, either intrinsically through strong coupling or via the application of a large magnetic field, and coexists with the disorder potential, its behavior changes significantly. The phase stiffness effectively prevents single-particle tunneling due to Pauli blocking. Notably, when the phase stiffness is relatively low and the system is in a dilute state, we find that the effects of on-site Pauli blocking and single-particle wave function scattering are mutually exclusive. However, at strong coupling, we discover that the system can be accurately described by a bosonic Hubbard model with a large, even integer on-site dispersion, thereby replicating a system of fermions.

Software test design flaws, known as test smells, can be perceived by some developers as not being severe enough to warrant attention. Understanding how developers perceive these smells can shed light on why they often go unnoticed. To investigate this matter, we conducted an empirical study involving Java developers, collecting data through a survey and interviews. The results showed that many developers do not perceive all test smells as severe, with some even believing that certain smells are desirable. Additionally, many developers who encountered test smells did not take appropriate action. Based on these findings, we propose that developers should be educated about the potential negative impacts of test smells and that existing detection tools should be enhanced to address how developers view these smells.

This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, initially proposed by J.J. Moreau in the early 1970s as part of plasticity theory. The proposed modification involves a novel combination of the original time-dependent differential equation and a time-continuous integro-differential equation, with nonconvex properties in a Hilbert space setting. By applying fixed point arguments, we establish that under specific conditions, the resulting integro-differential sweeping process has a single continuous solution. Furthermore, the obtained results have been successfully applied to two distinct practical scenarios, including dynamic network modeling and the study of elastomers with memory effects.

We present the $KKMCee$ event generator for lepton colliders, designed to simulate
lepton and quark pair production with associated photon emissions. Our program, built
upon the renowned $KKMC$ algorithm, has been adapted to exclude hadronization and
quark gluon splitting. It was compared to other established generators, with results
showing minimal differences. The $JJMCee$ and $PYTHIA6ee$ generators exhibited a
slightly harder lepton angle distribution, whereas the $KKMCee$ generator with PHOTOS
produced a similar outcome. In contrast, comparisons with $HERA7`ee` show a slightly
harder photon spectrum with a corresponding $\sim0.1\%$ discrepancy at $300$ GeV.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals is a critical component of various biomedical applications such as diagnosing heart conditions and monitoring patients. A new approach is introduced to accurately estimate inter-beat intervals from noisy, real-world ECG signals. The method involves a two-step process: peak detection and interval calculation, utilizing the recently developed Tiramisu model for peak detection. By using pixel-based CNN for peak detection and a simple moving average filter for interval calculation, this approach achieves high accuracy. Comprehensive testing was conducted on the MIT-BIH database using multiple techniques including R-peaks, linear regression, and correlation coefficient analysis. Results show that our proposed method surpasses other techniques by demonstrating superior performance with lower error rates and minimal bias, particularly when employing RGB channels for peak detection.

This paper introduces a randomized algorithm for computing the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) in low tensor ranks. Given a three-dimensional tensor and an approximation tolerance, the algorithm ensures that with high certainty it will return the t-SVD factors within the specified tolerance after a single pass or after multiple passes. A key aspect of the proof relies on a newly established Bretschneider-type inequality for three-way tensors in the sub-Gaussian setting. To validate the practical effectiveness of the proposed method, we conducted a comprehensive experiment comparing our algorithm to existing greedy methods for tensor decomposition. The results demonstrate that a few iterations of the randomized algorithm yield superior performance.

Network analysis has seen significant advancements through the application of embedding techniques, which allow for the representation of complex network structures in lower-dimensional space. Traditionally, graph embeddings focused on capturing static network topologies, but with the increasing importance of modeling dynamic graph patterns, new challenges have emerged. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of approaches and methods for embedding dynamic graphs, highlighting the latest research and existing challenges. By examining the motivations, definitions, and solutions of these approaches, the aim is to provide a unified framework and facilitate future research. A detailed comparison of these approaches is also provided, along with an analysis of their strengths and limitations.

Our investigation into a $^7$H resonance focuses on it being the ground state of $^7$Li with four neutrons. By analyzing the two-neutron separation energy in $^7$H, we are able to determine the mass of $^7$H, and in turn, the $^3$H-$^4$O relative threshold. Utilizing the Resonating Group Method to calculate the potential energy surface and the R-matrix approach to extract the two-neutron separation energy, we find that $^7$H is a $^7$Li + 4 neutron resonance located approximately 1.1 MeV below the $^3$H-$^4$O threshold and approximately 2.3 MeV above the neutron emission threshold, with the width of approximately 2.3 MeV, which is consistent with the findings of the first direct observation of the $^7$H resonance in a $^6$He + $^9$Be reaction reported in 2020.

This research paper focuses on solving the Nirenberg problem on the upper half spheres, with the goal of finding blow-up solutions to a Poisson equation with boundary conditions. The function of these solutions includes all critical values of the spherical reciprocal area. However, beyond the primary eigenvalue, there are numerous non-simple eigenvalues associated with it. Utilizing full Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction methods, it is demonstrated that a single type of each corresponding eigenspace is present, with the goal manifolds exhibiting the structure of high-dimensional spheres.

Deep Metric Learning methods typically rely on a hand-crafted embedding with a fixed structure, as well as a task-specific, inter-class divergence loss designed to mitigate dataset biases. To overcome these limitations, this work suggests the use of Sinkhorn Divergences, leveraging their ability to generalize across datasets, and proposes the Deep-OSE loss, a novel approach that combines mini-batch and semi-supervised objectives. This new loss function reconfigures the embedding as a trainable, step-by-step structure called an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck step, thus enhancing discriminative power. The results show that Deep-OSE outperforms existing Deep Metric Learning methods on image, audio, and graph data for semi-supervised learning tasks.

In various fields of public health, partnerships between government agencies and private organizations are becoming increasingly common. They often collaborate to achieve shared public health goals, a practice that has the potential to be driven by multiple motivations, including practical reasons. A notable example is the local tracing partnerships established in England for COVID-19 contact tracing, a public health initiative. These partnerships, where smaller authorities with existing door-to-door tracing experience assumed responsibility for contact tracing within their territories, were formed in 2020 when 69 out of 152 government-approved agencies began working alongside NHS Test and Trace in the same month it launched. Our study investigates the potential positive influence of these partnerships by comparing the door-to-door tracing performance of partnered and non-partnered units using comprehensive data from all government-approved COVID-19 contact tracing units. We discovered significant disparities in the performance of these units, and the partnerships appeared to provide a substantial performance advantage.

Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a vital component of astrophysical research.  Utilizing the Gaia Data Release 2,  we have obtained precise sky coordinates, proper motion, and brightness data for cluster members and field stars surrounding the open cluster Melotte 72.  Through our creation of a member catalog,  we have derived key properties of the cluster,  including its distance,  age,  and gravity radius,  and found a discrepancy between our results and previous studies of the cluster's age.  Furthermore,  we have determined the line of nodes and line of apses angles for the cluster's orbit.  We have also compared the cluster's density distribution and kinematics to those of other nearby clusters.

Guillemin and Kirsch's 2016 work introduced an elegant method to count critical points in Gaussian paths with specified Betti numbers. Building upon their results, we extend this to sparse excursions where the parameter $s$ approaches zero, specifically focusing on the range $0\leqslant s\leqslant 1/2$. As $s$ approaches zero, the system undergoes a phase transition at $s_c=1/4$, and we demonstrate that the Betti numbers exhibit distinct asymptotic behaviors: for $0\leqslant s<1/4$, the Betti numbers tend towards zero, while for $1/2\geqslant s>1/4$, they approach a constant value, $1-s$. Moreover, the Betti numbers of order $k$ experience a phase transition at $s_{k}=1/(k+2)$, characterized by a sharp transition from zero to $1$ as $s$ surpasses $1/(k+2)$. To achieve these findings, we utilize a non-perturbative approach that relies on solving a cubic equation, along with an efficient method to calculate action values at critical points. Our results are further validated by numerical simulations that cover both the dense and sparse regimes.

In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has long been a limiting factor, especially when it comes to accessing the camera's origin and direction. The problem is particularly challenging as most traditional methods require manual manipulation of the camera, which is not always feasible in real-world applications. To address this issue, we propose an image-based methodology that determines the camera's parameters in an image without requiring additional tools or image acquisition. Our method, grounded in projective geometry, is verified through image analysis of checkerboard patterns and supported by newly collected data sets, which include the camera's position in an image. Experimental results of our approach in real-world scenarios confirm its effectiveness in determining the camera's parameters.

A key issue in reinforcement learning involves specifying a task for an agent. This paper introduces a novel, inverse-constrained formulation of reinforcement learning that leverages expert demonstrations, not for deriving constraints, but for informing the agent of tasks it should complete. Our approach leverages demonstration trajectories to set up an RCRL problem by employing importance sampling, enabling the agent to efficiently allocate its computational resources across different tasks. We evaluate our method against notable existing reinforcement learning and constrained reinforcement learning algorithms on benchmark tasks. Our evaluation demonstrates that, on many tasks, our RCRL formulation surpasses the performance of prominent algorithms.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D chart of the galaxy by studying a significant number of stars with high accuracy in position, movement, and brightness. This will enable scientists to map the galaxy in three dimensions and study its formation and future evolution. This article provides an overview of the scientific questions driving GAIA, the challenges it faces, and a summary of the mission's design and data analysis methods. It also outlines potential breakthrough discoveries and their impact on our understanding of the galaxy.

For graphs with a given number of vertices and treewidth of order $O(n^{1/2-\epsilon})$, we have devised a word-RAM algorithm to compute minimum vertex separators in $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon'})$ time with high probability, effectively reducing the time complexity while maintaining efficiency. This algorithm further generalizes to tolerate an $O(n^{1/2-\epsilon})$ bound for treewidth, achieving $O(n^{1+\epsilon'})$ time in the worst case, where the value of $\epsilon'$ approaches zero as the graph size approaches infinity. These findings directly enhance the performance of dynamic treewidth algorithms, specifically reducing the time complexity to construct and modify partial tree-decompositions, and specifically for the update operation, reducing the time complexity to $O(m^{1/2+\epsilon'})$ where $m$ is the number of edges in the graph.

The identification of groups within data is a fundamental aspect of various fields, particularly within the study of complex networks. One widely used method for classifying networks involves partitioning their elements into distinct groups. OneKeyClust, a recently developed approach, utilizes an optimization technique to identify meaningful clusters based on the connections within a network. This approach is versatile and can be applied to networks with both positive and negative relationships, as well as those with different types of interactions. This study provides an in-depth analysis of one key variant of OneKeyClust, exploring its implications for network interpretation and highlighting how its behavior changes under different types of network interactions. By incorporating both analytical and visual methods, the research demonstrates how OneKeyClust can be used to identify clusters in networks with both positive and negative relationships. Furthermore, the study examines how the choice of oneKeyClust's parameters affects the outcomes of the analysis and discusses potential future directions for the method.

To enhance the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), a new technique has been developed for estimating their errors and obtaining guaranteed error bounds. This method is referred to as a posteriori error estimation and can confirm the correctness of a PINN's results within predetermined error limits. The approach utilizes a trained PINN to calculate the errors in a PinNN, using the differences between the PINN and itself, adjusted in a specific way, to obtain the errors and confirm its results. The approach can be applied in situations where the training process is completed and can be implemented efficiently and automatically. The approach has two key components: one that estimates the errors and another that ensures the errors do not amplify when calculating the PINN's outputs. The approach has been tested for PINNs involving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and partial differential equations (PDEs) to obtain accurate solutions and confirm their results.

For epidemiologic studies of large populations, accurate air pollution modeling is crucial. Leveraging machine learning capabilities can enhance this process by supplementing and analyzing measured data more effectively than conventional approaches. The main objective of this study is to evaluate the present air pollution modeling methods used in epidemiology, focusing on the integration of geostatistics and machine learning methods, along with the resulting models. Additionally, it will explore the application of various algorithms for downscaling high-resolution satellite readings. Models generated through geostatistics, machine learning, and a hybrid method will be examined. Using real-world measurements, we assessed model performance based on key evaluation criteria including mean squared error, data coverage, and continuity of resulting fields. Our study utilized 2018 air quality measurements from the California Department of Public Health to evaluate the accuracy of air quality models for a target population in that state. Results indicated that machine learning models, specifically the kriging model, performed better than their counterparts.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes (such as Avron-Schick states or trivial zero modes), it is crucial to develop methods that can identify the Majorana peak uniquely. This study suggests an method using tunneling spectroscopy with ohmic dissipation by inserting a resistive layer (made of an oxide) in contact with a Majorana superconductor. The resulting tunneling spectra at the zero-energy show distinct patterns between topological and non-topological contacts, providing a potential solution to distinguish between these peaks.

In linear bandits, we develop strategies for efficiently exploring action spaces with large sizes by introducing a new method that focuses on the most unpredictable areas and takes into account any differences in uncertainty across actions. We prove that our method leads to near optimal performance in experiments involving large action spaces and show that it leads to sound statistical conclusions in a controlled setting. We also successfully apply our algorithm to a real-world drug discovery challenge, achieving significant improvements in identifying effective treatments.

Graphene with gaps has been proposed to exhibit the valley Hall effect due to its unique properties, and in theory, creating this effect could allow us to generate stable valley currents in graphene-based devices. Our study, however, reveals that the desired effect is challenging to achieve in practice. Instead, we identified a new phenomenon called the orbital Hall effect, which naturally occurs when there is imbalance in the curvature of the valence bands at different valleys. This effect can be observed by adjusting the magnetic field orientation and results in the production of a measurable transverse voltage in graphene with gaps. Our calculations confirm that this phenomenon is significant and could potentially be detected in experiments.

The growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning in the realm of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) necessitates a deeper understanding of their vulnerabilities to malicious attacks in graph-based data. A notable vulnerability lies in data poisoning attacks, where an adversary manipulates training data to induce GNNs to perform poorly. Unfortunately, little is known about how GNNs are susceptible to such attacks, largely due to limited research and a lack of appropriate evaluation metrics. Our research addresses this gap by introducing a reinforcement learning-based approach to simulate various types of data poisoning attacks on GNNs. This study explores the effects of attack strategies on node classification accuracy and integrity, while also providing insights into the most effective defense mechanisms against these vulnerabilities.

The process of matching entries from different star catalogs is a fundamental aspect of establishing a consistent celestial reference frame, which serves as the basis for studying the movements and behavior of celestial bodies across various studies. Researchers have developed both analytical and numerical solutions to tackle the matching problem. We investigated how a combination of astrometric and photometric data can be utilized to enhance the matching process by developing a new method that integrates these different types of information. When applied to a dataset of 217,343 entries from the Gaia DR2 catalog and another 217,343 entries from the 2MASS catalog, our approach successfully identified the pairs that correspond to one another, achieving an accuracy of 98.9 percent. We also evaluated the performance of our method under different conditions, specifically when there were uncertainties in the astrometric measurements and when there were band mismatches between the catalogs. We found that incorporating additional photometric information into the matching process can significantly improve its accuracy, even when there were uncertainties in the astrometric measurements and band mismatches.

Infinite graph sets $E$ within a finite group $G$ have been analyzed by various authors such as Halin, Wagner, and Peters, whose work forms the basis for several established theorems. These studies demonstrated the following: (1) if the size of the graph is sufficiently large and certain conditions are met, then there exists a vertex cover with a certain maximum size; (2) if the size of the graph is sufficiently large and certain conditions are met, then there exists a vertex cover which is also an independent set. The aim of this paper is to extend these results to hypergraphs of arbitrary rank $r\geq 2$, while also raising certain open questions.

Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured in comprehensive, structured formats known as ontologies. However, large, complex ontologies are difficult to comprehend and navigate due to the extensive associations between their components, particularly in fields like biology where interconnections are abundant. To address this challenge, a new visualization technique called OntoPlot has been developed. It represents associations in ontologies in a linear format, effectively reducing complexity while preserving key information. By using a limited set of colors to convey directionality, it further simplifies the display without compromising on the richness of the data. OntoPlot has been successfully tested with a small protein-related dataset and can be applied to any association-based ontology, demonstrating its potential for enhanced understanding and analysis.

We've been working on ending the gap between formulating a problem and its actual resolution by integrating an end-to-end approach to the Automatic Speech Recognition problem, which involves training a model that can translate spoken language into text directly. This method has its drawbacks though, including the need for large, well-labeled datasets, which are time-consuming and costly to assemble. To alleviate this issue, we've been working on semi-supervised end-to-end Automatic Speech Recognition by using techniques derived from computer vision, such as using unlabeled data that's already available to their advantage. We've been focusing on two areas: a) using an unsupervised model that can adapt between two datasets, which helps bridge the domain gap, and b) using a loss function to find relationships between unlabeled sequences and the acoustic models. We've been testing this new method on three datasets: based on news transcripts, based on speeches, and the Librispeech dataset. The results show that this end-to-end end-to-end model performs better than its fully supervised counterpart by significantly improving performance without the need for extensive human labeling.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living organisms interact with their surroundings, enabling them to adapt by continuously updating their understanding of the world and minimizing prediction discrepancies. This theory is closely linked to two key capabilities: exploring the environment to develop a precise model and exploiting that model to achieve optimal outcomes. This theory has recently been successfully integrated with deep reinforcement learning to automatically implement active inference principles. This study presents a novel approach that combines deep active inference with convolutional attention mechanisms to efficiently process complex visual inputs for robot navigation. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach excels on the ALFRED benchmark, a real-world SLIM task that simulates a remote-controlled robot in an immersive VR environment, tasked with following multi-step instructions and executing instructed actions.

Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations out of equilibrium to explore the Soret effect. We discovered the potential Soret coefficient can be expressed as a sum of kinetic and thermodynamic components. The outcome of these components relies on whether molecules are hard or flexible. For hard molecules, we found both components agree. Conversely, for flexible molecules, the dominant degree of freedom determines the Soret effect, and we found the thermal cross-effect factor D12 is influenced by the molecular stiffness.

The development of Automated Essay Scoring (AES) systems has been ongoing for 50 years, with the primary challenge being the efficient evaluation of an essay's quality within a limited time frame. Effective AES systems should consider two essential components: content score and language use score, which typically require substantial human input for training. Due to the scarcity of high-quality training data, recent advancements in transformer-based models have enabled the development of more efficient training data generation methods and AES systems with reduced resource requirements. In this research, a novel data augmentation technique is presented that enhances the training process for AES by incorporating synthetic reviews and generating additional training data through knowledge distillation. By using this method, a nGram n-gram cross entropy (nGCE) model is able to achieve state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets, including the 2018 JED dataset, achieving a correlation of 0.8342, and outperforming other AES systems on the 2018 Chinese EES dataset, with a correlation of 0.5062.
